problem: "whenever he chose" sharpens source "upon occasions"; added "Even"; "State" should be lowercase "state" (political body) per STYLE-NOTE.
replacement: While I was in the United States, I noticed that a democratic state of society like the Americans’ might offer unusual openings for establishing despotism. After I returned to Europe, I saw how much most of our rulers had already exploited the ideas, feelings, and needs that this same social condition produces, in order to widen the reach of their power. This made me think that the nations of Christendom might in time suffer some kind of oppression like the one that once weighed on several nations of the ancient world. I have examined the subject more closely and thought about it for five more years. My fears have not lessened, but they now point at a different object. In earlier ages, no sovereign was ever so absolute or so powerful that he tried to administer every part of a great empire by his own agency, without intermediate powers to help him. None ever tried to bind all his subjects, without distinction, to a strict uniformity of regulation, or to tutor and direct each member of the community in person. Such an undertaking never occurred to the human mind. And had anyone conceived it, the lack of information, the flaws of the administrative system, and above all the natural obstacles that the inequality of conditions created would soon have stopped so vast a design from being carried out. When the Roman emperors were at the height of their power, the different nations of the empire kept very diverse customs and ways of life. Though all were subject to the same monarch, most of the provinces were administered separately, and they were full of strong and active municipalities. And although the whole government of the empire was concentrated in the emperor’s hands, and he remained, on occasion, the final arbiter in every matter, the details of social life and of private occupations were for the most part beyond his control. It is true that the emperors held an immense and unchecked power, which let them indulge every whim and use the whole strength of the state for that purpose. They often abused this power arbitrarily, taking away their subjects’ property or lives. Their tyranny weighed very heavily on a few people, but it did not reach the majority. It fixed on a handful of main objects and ignored the rest; it was violent, but its range was limited.

problem: "I expect rather guardians" adds an assertion of his own; source only says he has no fear of tyrants but rather of guardians.
replacement: Apart from these reasons, which come from the nature of the social state itself, I could add many others that arise from causes outside my subject, but I will stay within the limits I have set for myself. Democratic governments may turn violent and even cruel in times of extreme agitation or great danger, but such crises will be rare and short. When I consider the petty passions of our contemporaries, the mildness of their customs, the breadth of their education, the purity of their religion, the gentleness of their morality, their orderly and hardworking habits, and the restraint that almost all of them show in their vices as well as in their virtues, I have no fear that they will find tyrants in their rulers, but rather guardians. *a I think, then, that the kind of oppression threatening democratic nations is unlike anything that has existed in the world before; our contemporaries will find no precedent for it in their memories. I am trying to find a word that would convey the whole idea I have formed of it, but I try in vain. The old words “despotism” and “tyranny” do not fit; the thing itself is new, and since I cannot name it, I must try to define it.

problem: "the State" (political body) should be lowercase "the state" per STYLE-NOTE.
replacement: What did most to protect the independence of private persons in aristocratic ages was that the supreme power did not claim to take the government and administration of the community wholly on itself. Those functions were necessarily left in part to the members of the aristocracy. Since the supreme power was always divided, it never pressed with its whole weight, or in the same way, on each individual. Not only did the government not do everything through its own direct agency. Most of the agents who carried out its duties drew their power not from the state but from their birth, and so they were not under its constant control. The government could not make or unmake them in an instant at its pleasure, or bend them into strict uniformity to its slightest whim. This was a further guarantee of private independence. I readily admit that we cannot turn to the same means today, but I find certain democratic expedients that may take their place. Instead of placing in the government alone all the administrative powers taken from corporations and nobles, some of them can be entrusted to secondary public bodies, made up temporarily of private citizens. In this way the liberty of individuals will be more secure, and their equality will not be reduced.

problem: "what the State accomplishes" should be lowercase "state" per STYLE-NOTE.
replacement: Before I close forever the subject that has held me so long, I would gladly take a last look over all the different features of modern society and finally weigh the general influence that the principle of equality will have on the fate of mankind. But the difficulty of the task stops me. Faced with so great an object, my sight is clouded and my reason fails. The society of the modern world, which I have tried to describe and now try to judge, has only just come into existence. Time has not yet given it its final shape. The great revolution that created it is not yet over, and amid the events of our day it is almost impossible to tell what will pass away with the revolution itself and what will outlast it. The world that is rising is still half burdened with the remains of the world that is sinking into decay. Amid the vast confusion of human affairs, no one can say how much of the old institutions and former customs will survive, or how much will disappear entirely. The revolution now under way in the social condition, the laws, the opinions, and the feelings of men is still very far from over. Even so, its results already cannot be compared with anything the world has seen before. I go back age by age to the most distant antiquity and find nothing like what is happening before my eyes. Since the past no longer lights the way into the future, the human mind wanders in the dark. Still, in the midst of a prospect so wide, so new, and so confused, some of the more prominent features can already be made out and pointed to. The good things and the evils of life are more evenly spread across the world. Great wealth tends to vanish and small fortunes to multiply. Desires and satisfactions increase, but extraordinary prosperity and hopeless poverty are equally unknown. The feeling of ambition is universal, but its scope is seldom large. Each individual stands apart in lonely weakness, while society as a whole is active, farsighted, and powerful. What private persons accomplish is insignificant; what the state accomplishes is immense. There is little energy of character, but customs are mild and laws are humane. There are few examples of lofty heroism or of the highest, brightest, and purest virtues, but men’s habits are orderly, violence is rare, and cruelty is almost unknown. Human life grows longer and property more secure. Life is not adorned with brilliant trophies, but it is very easy and peaceful. Few pleasures are either very refined or very coarse, and highly polished manners are as uncommon as great brutality of taste. One finds neither men of great learning nor communities of extreme ignorance. Genius grows rarer and information more widespread. The human mind is moved forward by the small efforts of all mankind combined, not by the strenuous activity of certain men. There is less perfection but more abundance in everything the arts produce. The ties of race, rank, and country are loosened, and the great bond of humanity is strengthened. If I try to find the most general and most prominent of all these features, I will see that what is happening to men’s fortunes appears in a thousand other forms. Almost all extremes are softened or blunted. Everything that stood out most is replaced by some middle term, at once less lofty and less low, less brilliant and less obscure, than what the world had known before.
